FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME (DBA) STATEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Custom Woodworking · Acme Enterprises, LLC

FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME STATEMENT — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This Fictitious Business Name Statement Information Sheet relates to the fictitious business name "Acme Custom Woodworking" used by Acme Enterprises, LLC, a limited liability company with a principal place of business at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, in connection with a filing made with the Clerk of San Francisco County. California law treats the use of a business name other than a person's or entity's own true legal name as a distinct filing event, addressed in Business and Professions Code Chapter 5 (Sections 17900 through 17930), commonly called a fictitious business name statement or, informally, a "DBA" filing. This is a county-level filing made with the clerk of the county where the business's principal place of business is located — it is not a state-level filing with the California Secretary of State. It is separate from, and does not substitute for, the state-level filings involved in forming a corporation or LLC (articles of incorporation or articles of organization) or in that entity's periodic Statement of Information filed with the Secretary of State after formation. An entity can complete all of those state-level filings and still separately need to file a fictitious business name statement at the county level if it uses a name other than the name already on file with the Secretary of State, just as an individual sole proprietor who has made no state-level filing at all can independently be required to file one. This document's research addressed only this county-level fictitious business name filing requirement under California's Business and Professions Code; it did not research the filing requirements of any other state, or any additional local business license or tax registration requirement that a county or city may separately impose on the same business.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A 'FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME'
California's fictitious business name statute defines what counts as a "fictitious business name" separately for each type of registrant — it is not simply any name a business chooses to operate under. For an individual, a name is fictitious if it does not include that individual's own surname, or if it suggests the existence of additional owners the individual does not actually have. For a partnership or other association of persons (with statutory exceptions for certain limited partnerships and registered limited liability partnerships that separately register with the Secretary of State), a name is fictitious if it does not include the surname of each general partner, or if it suggests additional owners beyond those partners. For a domestic or foreign corporation, any name other than the exact corporate name stated in its articles of incorporation on file with the Secretary of State is a fictitious business name. For a limited liability company, any name other than the exact name stated in its articles of organization on file with the Secretary of State is a fictitious business name. A name "suggests the existence of additional owners" if it includes words such as "Company," "& Company," "& Son," "& Sons," "& Associates," or "Brothers," though not words that merely describe the business being conducted. The statute states its own purpose directly: to protect people dealing with a business operating under a name other than its true name, by making the identity of the people or entity behind that name a matter of public record — and the statute expressly states it is not intended to confer any right or advantage on a business that files, or on one that fails to.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The purpose of this section is to protect those dealing with individuals or partnerships doing business under fictitious names, and it is not intended to confer any right or advantage on individuals or firms that fail to comply with the law. The filing of a fictitious business name certificate is designed to make available to the public the identities of persons doing business under the fictitious name."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(a)(1), Fictitious Business Names, statement of statutory purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17900.)
  "As used in this chapter, “fictitious business name” means: (1) In the case of an individual, a name that does not include the surname of the individual or a name that suggests the existence of additional owners, as described in subdivision (c). (2) In the case of a partnership or other association of persons, other than a limited partnership that has filed a certificate of limited partnership with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.01 of the Corporations Code, a foreign limited partnership that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15909.02 of the Corporations Code, a registered limited liability partnership that has filed a registration pursuant to Section 16953 of the Corporations Code, or a foreign limited liability partnership that has filed an application for registration pursuant to Section 16959 of the Corporations Code, a name that does not include the surname of each general partner or a name that suggests the existence of additional owners, as described in subdivision (c) and in Section 17901. (3) In the case of a domestic or foreign corporation, any name other than the corporate name stated in its articles of incorporation filed with the California Secretary of State, in accordance with subdivision (a) of Section 17910.5. (4) In the case of a limited partnership that has filed a certificate of limited partnership with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.01 of the Corporations Code and in the case of a foreign limited partnership that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.02 of the Corporations Code, any name other than the name of the limited partnership as on file with the California Secretary of State. (5) In the case of a limited liability company, any name other than the name stated in its articles of organization and in the case of a foreign limited liability company that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 17708.02 of the Corporations Code, any name other than the name of the limited liability company as on file with the California Secretary of State, in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 17910.5."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(b), Fictitious Business Names, statutory definition by registrant type (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17900.)
  "A name that suggests the existence of additional owners within the meaning of subdivision (b) is one that includes such words as “Company,” “& Company,” “& Son,” “& Sons,” “& Associates,” “Brothers,” and the like, but not words that merely describe the business being conducted."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(c), Fictitious Business Names, what it means for a name to 'suggest additional owners' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17900.)

All three citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900 — subdivisions (a)(1), (b), and (c) — and are treated as one source, not three independent statutes. This clause's research also confirmed the statute contains additional categories not summarized above: separate definitions for limited partnerships and foreign limited partnerships that have filed with the Secretary of State (subdivision (b)(4)), which this document's fields do not separately address because this project's scope, per its research request, targeted individuals, partnerships, corporations, and LLCs rather than limited partnerships specifically.

FILING DEADLINE AND WHERE THE STATEMENT IS FILED
A person or entity that regularly transacts business in California for profit under a fictitious business name is statutorily required to file a fictitious business name statement, and the statute sets a deadline measured from when that business under the name actually began: the statement must be filed not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences transacting business under the fictitious name. The statement is not filed with the California Secretary of State. It is filed at the county level, with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has its principal place of business in California; if the registrant has no place of business in California, the statement is instead filed with the Clerk of Sacramento County. California law also permits, without requiring, filing in a county other than the county of the principal place of business, so long as the filing in the principal-place-of-business county is also separately made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every person who regularly transacts business in this state for profit under a fictitious business name shall do all of the following: (a) File a fictitious business name statement in accordance with this chapter not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences to transact such business."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17910(a), Fictitious Business Names, the 40-day filing deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17910.)
  "A fictitious business name statement shall be filed with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has his or her principal place of business in this state or, if the registrant has no place of business in this state, with the Clerk of Sacramento County. This chapter does not preclude a person from filing a fictitious business name statement in a county other than that where the principal place of business is located, as long as the requirements of this section are also met."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17915, Fictitious Business Names, county of filing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17915.)

Bus. & Prof. Code § 17915 sets the county-level place of filing; each is an independent source.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF THE STATEMENT
California's statute prescribes a specific form of content for a fictitious business name statement rather than leaving the content to the filer's discretion. The statement must identify the fictitious business name or names used, the street address and county of the registrant's principal place of business, and — depending on what kind of registrant is filing — specific identifying information: an individual's full name; the full name of each general partner for a partnership; or, for an LLC or corporation, the entity's name and address exactly as stated in its articles of organization or articles of incorporation on file with the Secretary of State, together with its state of organization or incorporation. The statement must also state the nature of the business (for example, that the registrant is an individual, a partnership, an LLC, or a corporation) and the date the registrant commenced transacting business under the fictitious name. The registrant must sign a declaration that all information in the statement is true and correct, and the prescribed form itself states — as a matter of statute, not merely as boilerplate — that a registrant who declares as true a material matter under this statute knowing it to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The fictitious business name statement shall contain all of the information required by this subdivision and shall be substantially in the following form: FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME STATEMENT The following person (persons) is (are) doing business as * at ** : *** This business is conducted by **** The registrant commenced to transact business under the fictitious business name or names listed above on ***** I declare that all information in this statement is true and correct. (A registrant who declares as true any material matter pursuant to Section 17913 of the Business and Professions Code that the registrant knows to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000).)"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(a), Fictitious Business Names, prescribed statutory form and the false-declaration misdemeanor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17913.)
  "If the registrant is a limited liability company, insert the name and business mailing address of the limited liability company, as set out in its articles of organization on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of organization. If the registrant is a trust, insert the full name and business mailing address of each trustee. If the registrant is a corporation, insert the name and address of the corporation, as set out in its articles of incorporation on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of incorporation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(b)(3), Fictitious Business Names, registrant-identifying information by entity type (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17913.)

The quoted subdivision (b)(3) excerpt below also names trusts as a distinct registrant category with their own content requirement (naming each trustee), which this document's fields do not separately collect because trusts as fictitious-name registrants were outside this research's requested scope.

THE NEWSPAPER PUBLICATION REQUIREMENT
Filing a fictitious business name statement with the county clerk is not, by itself, the end of the statutory process — California also requires the statement to be published. Within 45 days after the statement has been filed, the registrant must cause it to be published in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the statement was filed (or, if no such newspaper exists in that county, in an adjoining county; or, for a registrant with no California place of business, in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County). The publication itself must run once a week for four successive weeks, under the state's general publication-of-notice statute, which specifies that four weekly publications with at least five days between each publication date are sufficient, with the notice period running from the first day of publication through the twenty-eighth day. After publication is complete, an affidavit showing that the statement was published must be filed with the same county clerk within 45 days after the publication is finished. A refiling made because a prior statement expired does not have to be republished, provided the information has not changed and the refiling is made within 40 days of the prior statement's expiration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Within 45 days after a fictitious business name statement has been filed pursuant to this chapter, the registrant shall cause a statement in the form prescribed by subdivision (a) of Section 17913 to be published pursuant to Section 6064 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the fictitious business name statement was filed or, if there is no such newspaper in that county, in a newspaper of general circulation in an adjoining county. If the registrant does not have a place of business in this state, the notice shall be published in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17917(a), Fictitious Business Names, publication deadline and newspaper selection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17917.)
  "An affidavit showing the publication of the statement shall be filed with the county clerk where the fictitious business name statement was filed within 45 days after the completion of the publication."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17917(d), Fictitious Business Names, filing the affidavit of publication (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17917.)
  "Publication of notice pursuant to this section shall be once a week for four successive weeks. Four publications in a newspaper regularly published once a week or oftener, with at least five days intervening between the respective publication dates not counting such publication dates, are sufficient. The period of notice commences with the first day of publication and terminates at the end of the twenty-eighth day, including therein the first day."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 6064, General Provisions Relating to Publication of Notice, the once-a-week-for-four-weeks requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=6064.)

EXPIRATION AND REFILING
A fictitious business name statement does not remain effective indefinitely. Absent an earlier expiration, it expires five years from the date it was filed with the county clerk. It can expire sooner: it expires 40 days after any change occurs in the facts originally set forth in the statement, and it also expires whenever the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name it covered. The statutorily prescribed form itself is required to state the statement's expiration date. Filing a new fictitious business name statement before an existing one expires is how a registrant continues its filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Unless the statement expires earlier under subdivision (b) or (c), a fictitious business name statement expires five years from the date it was filed in the office of the county clerk."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(a), Fictitious Business Names, the five-year expiration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17920.)
  "Except as provided in Section 17923, a fictitious business name statement expires 40 days after any change in the facts set forth in the statement pursuant to Section 17913."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(b), Fictitious Business Names, early expiration on a change of facts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17920.)
  "A fictitious business name statement expires when the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name described in the statement."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(c), Fictitious Business Names, expiration on a statement of abandonment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17920.)
  "Notice of the date of expiration shall be on the fictitious business name statement form."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17921, Fictitious Business Names, expiration date required on the form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17921.)

FILING DOES NOT CREATE EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS TO THE NAME
Filing a fictitious business name statement does not, by itself, authorize the use of that name in violation of another person's or entity's rights under federal, state, or common law — the statutorily prescribed form itself states this directly, in a notice that is required to appear on the form. Filing does have one narrower, related legal effect: California law establishes a rebuttable presumption that the first registrant to file a fictitious business name statement containing a given name in a particular county has the exclusive right to use that name, and any confusingly similar name, as a trade name within that county — but only for a registrant who is actually engaged in a trade or business using the name in that county, and only as a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, not a conclusive or automatic right. This presumption is a creature of this specific filing statute; it operates county by county rather than statewide, and it is separate from, and not a substitute for, federal or state trademark registration or the common-law trademark rights that can arise independently from a business's actual use of a name in commerce.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "THE FILING OF THIS STATEMENT DOES NOT OF ITSELF AUTHORIZE THE USE IN THIS STATE OF A FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME IN VIOLATION OF THE RIGHTS OF ANOTHER UNDER FEDERAL, STATE, OR COMMON LAW (SEE SECTION 14411 ET SEQ., BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONS CODE)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(a), Fictitious Business Names, statutory notice that filing does not authorize infringing use (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17913.)
  "The filing of any fictitious business name statement by a person required to file such statement pursuant to Section 17910 shall establish a rebuttable presumption that the registrant has the exclusive right to use as a trade name the fictitious business name, as well as any confusingly similar trade name, in the county in which the statement is filed, if the registrant is the first to file such a statement containing the fictitious business name in that county, and is actually engaged in a trade or business utilizing such fictitious business name or a confusingly similar name in that county. The rebuttable presumption created by this section shall be one affecting the burden of producing evidence."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14411, Trade Name Registration, the rebuttable presumption created by first-to-file (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14411.)

This document's research addressed only these two California statutes; it did not independently research federal trademark law (including the Lanham Act) or California common-law trademark doctrine, and any statement above about trademark rights existing independently of this filing describes only the fact that such rights can exist and does not characterize their scope, requirements, or how they would interact with a specific name in a specific case.

CONSEQUENCES OF TRANSACTING BUSINESS WITHOUT A VALID STATEMENT ON FILE
California law attaches two distinct consequences to the fictitious business name filing requirement. The first is civil: a person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the statute may not maintain any action in a California court on a contract made, or a transaction had, in that fictitious business name, until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as the statute requires. The statute carves out one specific exception: failing to satisfy the newspaper-selection preference in a different subdivision of the publication statute does not, by itself, count as "transacting business contrary to" the chapter for purposes of this civil consequence. The second consequence is criminal: any person who executes, files, or publishes a statement under this statutory chapter knowing that the statement is false, in whole or in part, is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable upon conviction by a fine of up to $1,000 — the same $1,000 figure the prescribed statement form separately references for a registrant who knowingly declares false material information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the provisions of this chapter, or his assignee, may maintain any action upon or on account of any contract made, or transaction had, in the fictitious business name in any court of this state until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as required by this chapter. For the purposes of this section, the failure to comply with subdivision (b) of Section 17917 does not constitute transacting business contrary to the provisions of this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17918, Fictitious Business Names, bar on maintaining a court action while noncompliant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17918.)
  "Any person who executes, files, or publishes any statement under this chapter, knowing that such statement is false, in whole or in part, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof shall be punished by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17930, Fictitious Business Names, misdemeanor for a knowingly false statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17930.)

expectedJSON.body: A person or entity that regularly transacts business in California for profit under a fictitious business name is statutorily required to file a fictitious business name statement, and the statute sets a deadline measured from when that business under the name actually began: the statement must be filed not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences transacting business under the fictitious name. The statement is not filed with the California Secretary of State. It is filed at the county level, with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has its principal place of business in California; if the registrant has no place of business in California, the statement is instead filed with the Clerk of Sacramento County. California law also permits, without requiring, filing in a county other than the county of the principal place of business, so long as the filing in the principal-place-of-business county is also separately made.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, the 40-day filing deadline
citations.quote: Every person who regularly transacts business in this state for profit under a fictitious business name shall do all of the following: (a) File a fictitious business name statement in accordance with this chapter not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences to transact such business.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, county of filing
citations.quote: A fictitious business name statement shall be filed with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has his or her principal place of business in this state or, if the registrant has no place of business in this state, with the Clerk of Sacramento County. This chapter does not preclude a person from filing a fictitious business name statement in a county other than that where the principal place of business is located, as long as the requirements of this section are also met.

expectedJSON.body: California's statute prescribes a specific form of content for a fictitious business name statement rather than leaving the content to the filer's discretion. The statement must identify the fictitious business name or names used, the street address and county of the registrant's principal place of business, and — depending on what kind of registrant is filing — specific identifying information: an individual's full name; the full name of each general partner for a partnership; or, for an LLC or corporation, the entity's name and address exactly as stated in its articles of organization or articles of incorporation on file with the Secretary of State, together with its state of organization or incorporation. The statement must also state the nature of the business (for example, that the registrant is an individual, a partnership, an LLC, or a corporation) and the date the registrant commenced transacting business under the fictitious name. The registrant must sign a declaration that all information in the statement is true and correct, and the prescribed form itself states — as a matter of statute, not merely as boilerplate — that a registrant who declares as true a material matter under this statute knowing it to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, prescribed statutory form and the false-declaration misdemeanor
citations.quote: The fictitious business name statement shall contain all of the information required by this subdivision and shall be substantially in the following form: FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME STATEMENT The following person (persons) is (are) doing business as * at ** : *** This business is conducted by **** The registrant commenced to transact business under the fictitious business name or names listed above on ***** I declare that all information in this statement is true and correct. (A registrant who declares as true any material matter pursuant to Section 17913 of the Business and Professions Code that the registrant knows to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000).)

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, registrant-identifying information by entity type
citations.quote: If the registrant is a limited liability company, insert the name and business mailing address of the limited liability company, as set out in its articles of organization on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of organization. If the registrant is a trust, insert the full name and business mailing address of each trustee. If the registrant is a corporation, insert the name and address of the corporation, as set out in its articles of incorporation on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of incorporation.

expectedJSON.body: Filing a fictitious business name statement with the county clerk is not, by itself, the end of the statutory process — California also requires the statement to be published. Within 45 days after the statement has been filed, the registrant must cause it to be published in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the statement was filed (or, if no such newspaper exists in that county, in an adjoining county; or, for a registrant with no California place of business, in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County). The publication itself must run once a week for four successive weeks, under the state's general publication-of-notice statute, which specifies that four weekly publications with at least five days between each publication date are sufficient, with the notice period running from the first day of publication through the twenty-eighth day. After publication is complete, an affidavit showing that the statement was published must be filed with the same county clerk within 45 days after the publication is finished. A refiling made because a prior statement expired does not have to be republished, provided the information has not changed and the refiling is made within 40 days of the prior statement's expiration.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, publication deadline and newspaper selection
citations.quote: Within 45 days after a fictitious business name statement has been filed pursuant to this chapter, the registrant shall cause a statement in the form prescribed by subdivision (a) of Section 17913 to be published pursuant to Section 6064 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the fictitious business name statement was filed or, if there is no such newspaper in that county, in a newspaper of general circulation in an adjoining county. If the registrant does not have a place of business in this state, the notice shall be published in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, filing the affidavit of publication
citations.quote: An affidavit showing the publication of the statement shall be filed with the county clerk where the fictitious business name statement was filed within 45 days after the completion of the publication.

citations.cite: General Provisions Relating to Publication of Notice, the once-a-week-for-four-weeks requirement
citations.quote: Publication of notice pursuant to this section shall be once a week for four successive weeks. Four publications in a newspaper regularly published once a week or oftener, with at least five days intervening between the respective publication dates not counting such publication dates, are sufficient. The period of notice commences with the first day of publication and terminates at the end of the twenty-eighth day, including therein the first day.

expectedJSON.body: A fictitious business name statement does not remain effective indefinitely. Absent an earlier expiration, it expires five years from the date it was filed with the county clerk. It can expire sooner: it expires 40 days after any change occurs in the facts originally set forth in the statement, and it also expires whenever the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name it covered. The statutorily prescribed form itself is required to state the statement's expiration date. Filing a new fictitious business name statement before an existing one expires is how a registrant continues its filing.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, the five-year expiration
citations.quote: Unless the statement expires earlier under subdivision (b) or (c), a fictitious business name statement expires five years from the date it was filed in the office of the county clerk.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, early expiration on a change of facts
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 17923, a fictitious business name statement expires 40 days after any change in the facts set forth in the statement pursuant to Section 17913.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, expiration on a statement of abandonment
citations.quote: A fictitious business name statement expires when the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name described in the statement.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, expiration date required on the form
citations.quote: Notice of the date of expiration shall be on the fictitious business name statement form.

expectedJSON.body: Filing a fictitious business name statement does not, by itself, authorize the use of that name in violation of another person's or entity's rights under federal, state, or common law — the statutorily prescribed form itself states this directly, in a notice that is required to appear on the form. Filing does have one narrower, related legal effect: California law establishes a rebuttable presumption that the first registrant to file a fictitious business name statement containing a given name in a particular county has the exclusive right to use that name, and any confusingly similar name, as a trade name within that county — but only for a registrant who is actually engaged in a trade or business using the name in that county, and only as a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, not a conclusive or automatic right. This presumption is a creature of this specific filing statute; it operates county by county rather than statewide, and it is separate from, and not a substitute for, federal or state trademark registration or the common-law trademark rights that can arise independently from a business's actual use of a name in commerce.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, statutory notice that filing does not authorize infringing use
citations.quote: THE FILING OF THIS STATEMENT DOES NOT OF ITSELF AUTHORIZE THE USE IN THIS STATE OF A FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME IN VIOLATION OF THE RIGHTS OF ANOTHER UNDER FEDERAL, STATE, OR COMMON LAW (SEE SECTION 14411 ET SEQ., BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONS CODE).

citations.cite: Trade Name Registration, the rebuttable presumption created by first-to-file
citations.quote: The filing of any fictitious business name statement by a person required to file such statement pursuant to Section 17910 shall establish a rebuttable presumption that the registrant has the exclusive right to use as a trade name the fictitious business name, as well as any confusingly similar trade name, in the county in which the statement is filed, if the registrant is the first to file such a statement containing the fictitious business name in that county, and is actually engaged in a trade or business utilizing such fictitious business name or a confusingly similar name in that county. The rebuttable presumption created by this section shall be one affecting the burden of producing evidence.

expectedJSON.body: California law attaches two distinct consequences to the fictitious business name filing requirement. The first is civil: a person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the statute may not maintain any action in a California court on a contract made, or a transaction had, in that fictitious business name, until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as the statute requires. The statute carves out one specific exception: failing to satisfy the newspaper-selection preference in a different subdivision of the publication statute does not, by itself, count as "transacting business contrary to" the chapter for purposes of this civil consequence. The second consequence is criminal: any person who executes, files, or publishes a statement under this statutory chapter knowing that the statement is false, in whole or in part, is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable upon conviction by a fine of up to $1,000 — the same $1,000 figure the prescribed statement form separately references for a registrant who knowingly declares false material information.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, bar on maintaining a court action while noncompliant
citations.quote: No person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the provisions of this chapter, or his assignee, may maintain any action upon or on account of any contract made, or transaction had, in the fictitious business name in any court of this state until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as required by this chapter. For the purposes of this section, the failure to comply with subdivision (b) of Section 17917 does not constitute transacting business contrary to the provisions of this chapter.

citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, misdemeanor for a knowingly false statement
citations.quote: Any person who executes, files, or publishes any statement under this chapter, knowing that such statement is false, in whole or in part, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof shall be punished by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000).
